item.title: Marine life in Gulf of Mexico has still not fully recovered from 2010 BP oil spill
item.description:
New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after the Deepwater Horizon spill

Marine life in the Gulf of Mexico plummeted by about 60% after BP’s 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill and has still not fully recovered, according to a new study.

The April 2010 explosion of an offshore drilling unit 50 miles off the Louisiana coast triggered the largest marine oil spill in history, releasing 134m gallons of oil into the ocean. According to the study published Monday in PNAS, the disaster – which also killed 11 people and injured 17 others – led to the “sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance” of marine life for more than a decade.

item.title: The town where Europe committed suicide
item.description:
Have you ever heard of Gorizia? Probably not, and yet it is decidedly pretty. It sits in the far north-eastern corner of Italy, where the Latin map frays into the Slavic. The centre is all pink arcades, pistachio green shutters, and palazzi painted in faded yellow. Beyond everything is the great pale wall of the Julian Alps.
The town has had at least three names - Gorizia, Görz, Gorica - because for centuries it was Habsburg, then Austro-Hungarian. That is to say: it was a quintessentially multilingual city, full of Italians, Slovenes, Friulians, Germans and Jews, halfway between Trieste and Vienna. Some called it the ‘Austrian Nice’. Imperial officials came here to die of tranquil old age.

item.description:
The closure of former WH Smith stores around the UK is sobering on many levels. The publications they sold were there to be perused, to broaden horizons

Towards the end of the 1970s, the brief but spectacular career of those punk rockers and folk devils the Sex Pistols was followed by The Great Rock’n’Roll Swindle, a rather tawdry drama-documentary. It recast their rise and fall as a huge scam, summed up by a slogan on a T-shirt worn by their former manager Malcolm McLaren: “Cash from Chaos”.

Back then, that motto was a neat representation of his personal brand of cultural mischief. But the culture always takes unexpected twists and turns – and 50 years on, an almost-identical maxim seems to be defining the fate of an increasing chunk of the British retail economy. While Andy Burnham pledges to restore life to town centres, a private equity outfit is busy buying up national retail chains and then shutting down scores of their outlets, while seemingly operating in line with its boss’s most celebrated quotation: “Where there’s chaos, there’s opportunity.”

item.title: ‘A hidden tradition’: Benjamin Moser wants you to know Jewish anti-Zionism is not new
item.description:
The writer rarely questioned the tenets of liberal Zionism growing up. Now he embraces anti-Zionism with the fervor of a new convert

In 1987, the Israeli human rights attorney Felicia Langer was paying a visit to the Neve Tirza women’s prison when a client named Siham shared some disturbing news: the prisoners held there had recently been sprayed with a chemical agent that left them writhing on the floor. Langer grabbed a tissue that had been exposed to the substance – a piece of evidence, perhaps, in a future legal case. Then, on impulse, she lifted it to her face and inhaled deeply. Her hope, she wrote later, was that doing so might enable a doctor to identify the toxin.

This anecdote appears in Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History, by Benjamin Moser. In it, the Pulitzer prize-winning author profiles a dozen Jews who actively opposed Zionism, before and after the establishment of Israel – from Aaron Samuel Tamares, a Polish rabbi who began inveighing against Jewish nationalism in the late 19th century; to British diplomat Edwin Montagu, who sought to derail the 1917 Balfour declaration promising a Jewish state in Palestine; to Israeli “new historian” Avi Shlaim – figures he sees as part of “a hidden tradition … of people who, though long dismissed and despised, were ultimately proven right”. Along the way, he seeks to dismantle the Zionist “fairytale,” as he puts it, piece by piece.

I saw a remarkable experiment take shape in Belgrade. Its lessons should be studied by other European countries struggling with unrest

More than a decade ago, the WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange told an interviewer in Belgrade that Serbia was “a country where the future happens first”. The phrase circulated widely on Serbian social media in the weeks before Sunday’s election, but in a way that could not have seemed possible 10 years ago. Who would then have imagined that Serbia today could be at the forefront of global democratic change?

The images from Belgrade on Sunday night – people dancing and crying in the streets, while in Novi Sad, the city that sparked the student movement, a flag bearing the image of the convicted war criminal Vojislav Šešelj, which had hung from a building since the 1990s, was torn down – reinforced the feeling that the future had truly arrived.

My parents began to worry that something was wrong, that my muscles were weaker than they should be. Eventually, at the age of three, I was diagnosed with a form of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). In the 1980s, the precise mechanics were not yet understood, but the condition was known to be hereditary, probably linked to a recessive gene. It was also known to be progressive. As I aged, my muscles would not keep pace. At eight, I began to use a wheelchair for longer distances. By the time I was 18, I rarely walked outdoors any more.

It is hard to be young and to know that you are growing weaker rather than stronger. I had all the same aspirations that my nondisabled friends did, but I lived in fear of the future in a way they did not. I spent a lot of time thinking about what my life would have been like if I didn’t have SMA. The images in my head were of something like a double: myself, only rid of this one deficit, imprecisely defined, but encoded somewhere in my body.

The worst kind of professional relationship is with the person you see twice a year, in a variety of different locations, because whatever they notice about you from that tiny observational sample, that’s what you’re like. So on the first rainy day in folk memory, the opening bars of Storm Austen, I turned up to a job with a photographer, soaked. I’d been on my bike and had tucked my trousers into my socks, so the accumulated water in the ankle area had seeped upwards, giving me a confusing wet leg-warmer effect, then a couple of dry inches, then an unbelievably wet rest of body. I was so wet that when I went to hug the studio’s labrador, he backed away from me like I was trying to give him a bath.

“You were really wet last time!” the photographer exclaimed, remembering our previous meeting back in March. “Well, it’s a wet country,” I replied, before the person we were there to shoot chipped in: “It’s actually in unprecedented drought, but fine.” Then the photographer asked, “Have you thought about getting some wet-weather clothes, if you’re going to cycle?” and I said, “Obviously this is the first time that’s occurred to me, otherwise it would have happened at some point between March and now,” except she didn’t hear me because I had my mouth full of Haribo chewy sours.

item.title: Anthropic’s 97-page list of business risks is quadruple the length of other AI IPOs. What’s on it: weapons, blackmail, and more
item.description:
In preparation for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever, Anthropic has finally filed its long-awaited prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission. That includes a summary of all the potential risks to Anthropic’s business, including both outside factors and threats from the AI company’s technology itself. Even keeping things concise, Anthropic’s list of risk factors came out to a whopping 97 pages long.

If nearly 100 pages of risks sounds like a lot, that’s because it is. Other recent AI companies to go public, including Roze AI, SpaceX, and QumulusAI, had risk disclosures just 21 pages long, 37 pages long, and 42 pages long, respectively.

Per the Code of Federal Regulations, if a business’s disclosure of risks exceeds 15 pages, it must include a bulleted list summarizing the main factors that make an investment in the company risky. Anthropic’s summary includes 18 bullet points, ranging from their own agents going rogue to the possibility of political turmoil.

Weaponized AI

Anthropic warns that its most advanced models have the potential to be abused by malicious actors (and already have been in the past). The company theorizes harmful uses for its AI models ranging in severity from “generating fraudulent or misleading content” to “perpetrating acts of violence” and developing “chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons.”

Though Anthropic notes that it has “technical safeguards” in place to avoid misuse, it admits that  “such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended.”

Agents gone wild

As Anthropic’s AI models get smarter, the company notes that they could go rogue, taking “harmful actions that no user or third party directed.” On a practical level, Anthropic says that might manifest as “committing code changes, deleting or modifying data, or completing financial transactions—before effective intervention is possible.”

Anthropic also notes that its models are increasingly being used in “high-risk or sensitive contexts,” including medicine, government, and law, where agents acting autonomously could prove especially harmful.

The company’s agents also have the potential to blackmail their users in the name of self-preservation. Anthropic says its models have exhibited “attempts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information, or generate outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative,” and they run the risk of doing so again.

Playing politics

Beyond its own technology, Anthropic cites the political landscape both domestically and internationally as a potential concern for would-be investors. Though Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has spoken out in favor of “pacing the frontier” to slow AI development, the company’s filing acknowledges that government regulation could also hamper its progress to the point of falling behind competitors, both technologically and strategically.

The backlash against data centers also poses a threat to Anthropic’s growth. The company notes moratoriums in states including Texas and New York that restrict data center development, reasoning that similar actions across the United States, where Anthropic’s data center infrastructure is currently concentrated, could disrupt its current operations. That’s why Anthropic is looking to expand its infrastructure internationally, though the filing notes that developing outside of the U.S. poses its own set of legal and operational risks.

item.title: Ozempic is changing how Americans spend money, and the numbers are startling
item.description:
Millions of Americans are spending potentially hundreds of dollars each month on GLP-1 medications, but that comes at a cost: Their weight-loss journey is shaking up how they spend their money.

In the five years since these medications were approved for chronic weight management by the Food and Drug Administration, they’ve grown in popularity to the point that an estimated 11% of American adults are now taking some form of glucagon-like peptide-1 medication to lose weight. While that’s led to some very visible trends—say, the protein-ification of many everyday foods—others aren’t so obvious.

Take jewelry, for example. 

The broader apparel industry has understandably benefited from the GLP-1 craze as 26% of users say they spend more on clothing overall, according to a survey conducted earlier this year by PwC. After being on the medication for six to eight months, many people seemingly adopt a “treat yourself” mentality, spending on higher-quality and more expensive brands, according to the report. While it makes sense that the weight-loss drug’s users are spending more on clothing—spending on jeans rose 66%, for example, while spending on swimwear was up 31%—it’s harder to account for why people are spending 36% more on jewelry.

And then there’s the impact on tailors. While the initial drop in weight can be good for business, many people end up regaining weight after they go off the medication—and that’s testing the free lifetime alterations offered by Brooklyn-based Alan David Custom, as Alan Horowitz, owner of the fifth-generation bespoke suit-maker business, told the Financial Times.

“The wild swings in weight  . . .  it’s been a tailoring nightmare,” Horowitz told the outlet.

THE WINNERS/LOSERS

The fitness industry likewise points to some contradictions. The PwC survey found that 36% of GLP-1 users are walking, running, cycling, and swimming more frequently, but they’ve perhaps become more selective about their workouts. In fact, 14% of people currently on these medications have decreased the frequency they’re attending group fitness classes, while only 11% have increased it.

Because doctors recommend strength training for patients on GLP-1 medications—to combat the loss of muscle mass or bone density during weight loss—that’s caused some gyms to reimagine their spaces. Chains like PureGym, Planet Fitness and the Gym Group have dedicated a greater share of floorspace to strength and functional training, as The Financial Times reported.

The airline industry is another such example. If the 178 passengers on a Boeing 737 plane were to lose 10% of their body weight, that would add up to about $580 million in combined savings each year for American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Southwest Airlines, and United Airlines, as Sheila Kahyaoglu, an analyst at Jefferies, calculated earlier this year. 

Given that airlines are always trying to contain costs, the savings could be significant, as Kahyaoglu told the Financial Times. “It actually could move the needle, especially because oil is so high right now.”

But even if a slimmed-down populace might be more prone to travel, they might be less likely to indulge in buying snacks or alcohol in-flight, as the outlet reported.

A MIXED BAG ON FOOD

Some of the biggest shifts in how Americans are spending their money is on food.

Quick-service restaurants are among the casualties of the GLP-1 era as household spending at these establishments fell nearly 9% after 6 to 8 months on the medication. And that weekly pizza night is especially out of favor, as spending fell 22% in that same timeframe. 

Grocery store sales also look different, as the PwC survey found that 61% of current GLP-1 users are buying fewer sweet treats, while sales of sugary drinks and alcohol also suffer. People are still headed to the grocery store, of course, but their carts look a bit different. Americans on these meds are spending more time on the perimeters—44% say they’re buying more fresh produce, while 34% are buying more fresh protein—and they’re opting for healthier items, like Greek yogurt, jerky or nutrition bars.

Those spending habits show that people are taking their weight-loss journey seriously while on the medications, even if many struggle to keep the weight off after they go off them.

“It’s perhaps not a surprise that people who are willing to pay this much for their health through GLP-1s will also pay more for healthier and better options,” Saxon Moseley, head of leisure and hospitality at accounting firm RSM UK, told the Financial Times.

item.title: The Guardian view on Israel’s elections: Netanyahu lost his mandate. If opponents unite, he’ll lose power too | Editorial
item.description:
His chief rival should reject the prime minister’s anti-democratic vision and work with Palestinian Israeli parties

Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his mandate but not, so far, power. While final votes are still being tallied, most voters picked his opponents on Tuesday. His bloc’s share of seats remains the largest, but appears to have slumped by around 10, leaving it below the 61 needed for a majority in the Knesset. Palestinian Israeli parties surged, and are projected to almost double the 10 seats they held. The result is that Mr Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the military, now faces a choice: fall into line with Mr Netanyahu’s racist fearmongering or work with Arab-led parties.

The prime minister who oversaw shocking security failures ahead of the Hamas atrocities of 7 October 2023 still pitches himself as “Mr Security”. On trial for corruption, he has persistently attacked democratic institutions, especially the judiciary. He embraced and then indulged the ultra-right as they cheered on brutal settler violence in the occupied West Bank. (Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich lost ground in these polls, but perhaps due to their vision’s permeation of mainstream politics more than a revolt against it.) Mr Netanyahu’s war on Iran has destabilised the region. The tens of thousands of Palestinians killed by his government’s genocidal war on Gaza have barely featured in the election campaign, but its cost for Israeli hostages and international support for Israel have been noted by voters.

item.title: The Amazon rainforest, long known as the ‘lungs of our planet,’ now releases more carbon than it absorbs
item.description:
The Amazon rainforest has long been called the “lungs of our planet,” because of how it takes in and stores billions of tons of carbon dioxide. 

But the Amazon has been losing that ability. Years of deforestation, drought, and fires have hindered just how much CO2 the rainforest can absorb. 

Now, the Amazon rainforest often releases more carbon than it takes in, a new study finds. It’s only in the “wettest years” that the rainforest is nearly carbon neutral.

The study, published in the journal Nature, was led by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research and included an international team of researchers. They used 15 years of atmospheric carbon measurements, which had been collected by research planes.

Those years were then grouped by different characteristics, like the level of human activities—which includes deforestation, logging, or using fires to clear land—and the amount of climate stress—like drought or heat waves. 

What the research found

Some years were wet with low human activity, some had low climatic stress but high human activity, and others had “intense global climate events, such as El Niño” along with intense amounts of human activity. 

In the years where the rainforest stayed relatively wet, and where there was relatively low deforestation and few wildfires, the Amazon was nearly carbon neutral. The forest was still a slight source of carbon into the atmosphere, but it “did not significantly contribute to the global carbon balance” in those years, the researchers write.

When drought or heat were mild but deforestation and wildfires occurred more, the net carbon emissions from the Amazon “jumped dramatically,” according to a statement. 

The years with lots of climate stress coupled with lots of damaging human activity were the worst. But they were still close to the net emissions from the second group, which led researchers to say that most of the carbon emitted by the Amazon comes from human activities, predominantly land-use change.

“Global climate and climate-mediated stressors are important modulating factors, but people’s choices about how to use and live on the land surface in this region are key to understanding the movement of carbon between the land and the atmosphere,” says coauthor Jen Johnson, assistant professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Kansas, in a statement. 

This isn’t the first paper to point out that the Amazon is not the grand carbon sink it once was. A 2021 study looked at how, as huge areas of the forest are cut down or burned, its ability to capture carbon was shrinking. 

In 2023, a year of extreme drought and high temperatures, researchers showed how the Amazon became a source of carbon emissions, releasing between 10 and 170 million tons of carbon instead of absorbing it. 

Slow burn

We’ve also long known that human activity is threatening the Amazon’s survival. In 2019, there were more than 74,000 fires burning in Brazil, mostly in the Amazon—80% more than the year before.

And though we often think of these as “wildfires,” they’re primarily set by ranchers who are clearing land for cattle to meet the demand for beef.  

The more deforestation, we know, the drier the Amazon becomes, which makes it even more difficult for the remaining parts of the forest to recover. 

“For many decades, there has been concern about the idea of a tipping point, where gradual drying and gradual loss of the forest could feed back on itself in a self-reinforcing way,” Johnson said.

“That could create a transition from an ecosystem type that has stored huge amounts of carbon in living vegetation to drier forests or other ecosystem types that do not store nearly as much carbon,” she continued. “The more carbon from the Amazon that moves into the atmosphere and stays there, the more trouble our climate system is in.”

Though the outlook is dire if these activities continue, the researchers say that policy changes can help. 

“There’s a clear, policy-relevant prescription that comes from this analysis,” Johnson said. “Measures to bring deforestation down to zero are required to manage net carbon emissions from the Amazon . . . It’s not something that’s out of our control because it’s being driven by global climatic factors—it’s something very much under the control of governments and individuals.”

item.title: Inside giant homebuilder D.R. Horton’s bet on robotic homebuilding
item.description:
Want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox? Subscribe to the ResiClub newsletter.

D.R. Horton, the nation’s largest homebuilder by volume, has signed a multi-year commercial agreement with Promise Robotics to use the startup’s robotic factory capacity on more than 1,250 homes. The deal, announced October 13, makes D.R. Horton the first major U.S. builder to sign on to Promise Robotics’ Factory-as-a-Service model.

On a typical jobsite, framing crews build walls by hand, cutting studs, nailing them together and standing them up on the foundation. That labor-intensive, weather-dependent work is where builders feel labor shortages most. Promise Robotics moves much of the framing into a factory, where robots assemble wall panels from the builder’s existing plans. The panels are then trucked to the site and set in place, which is far faster than framing from scratch.

D.R. Horton closed 84,863 homes in fiscal 2025, so the around 1,250 homes planned with Promise Robotics amount to about 1.5% of a single year’s volume. To start, this looks more like a measured test than a wholesale shift in how D.R. Horton builds.

In metro Phoenix, where Promise Robotics tells ResiClub all the 1,250 homes will be built and located, it’s a different story: 1,250 homes is more than half a year of D.R. Horton’s recent annual combined closings across Maricopa, Pinal, and Pima counties. The structure of the deal matters, too. D.R. Horton isn’t buying robots or building a factory. It’s renting automated production capacity from a third party that owns the plants, the software and the robotics, and that says it can now replicate the model market by market, starting with a factory in Gilbert, Arizona.

The deal

Under the agreement, D.R. Horton will tap Promise Robotics’ production platform to help build 1,250-plus homes. The companies did not disclose financial terms, a delivery timeline, or which Phoenix communities the homes will go to.

Brad Conlon, D.R. Horton’s senior vice president of strategic growth and innovation, framed the deal around three operating goals: faster cycle times, more production capacity, and more consistency and predictability. He called Promise Robotics’ platform a new capability for pursuing those goals.

How Factory-as-a-Service works

Promise Robotics’ pitch is that builders shouldn’t have to own a factory to get factory-style production. Under its Factory-as-a-Service model, Promise Robotics owns and runs the plants, robotics and software, and builders buy output.

The workflow runs in four steps:

  1. Design translation: Promise Robotics’ AI ingests a builder’s existing home plans, so the builder doesn’t have to redesign product for the factory.
  2. Production planning: The software generates production plans and machine instructions for the robots.
  3. Robotic manufacturing: Off-the-shelf industrial robots produce building components on the factory line.
  4. Site installation: Promise Robotics coordinates delivery and installation of those components on the jobsite.

The company says the integration is the differentiator: rather than automating one task, such as nailing or cutting, it ties design, factory and jobsite into a single production system. Earlier coverage of the company describes its output as framing components such as wall panels, though the D.R. Horton announcement doesn’t specify which components are in scope.

That asset-light structure matters for builders. Offsite construction has a long history of builders and startups sinking capital into factories that then sat underutilized when local demand cooled. Promise Robotics CEO Ramtin Attar made the same point back in 2023, when Promise Robotics raised a $15 million Series A: builders are reluctant to invest in costly factories and then spend years on trial and error.

From Edmonton to Calgary to Phoenix

Speaking to ResiClub, Attar laid out how Promise Robotics sees its path from Canadian pilot to U.S. scale:

“Promise is building the production infrastructure homebuilding scales on. Builders are increasingly looking to secure industrial production capacity through multi-year commitments because they need to deliver more homes with faster, more predictable cycle times. But building and operationalizing that capacity takes significant capital, time and expertise. Our platform removes those barriers: it turns a builder’s designs into production instructions, orchestrates production, and gets better with every build. We proved the model in Edmonton and scaled it in Calgary, where we’ve been in continuous production since September 2025. Now we’re replicating that model in Phoenix, creating the template for every market that follows.”

The Canadian track record is still short. Promise Robotics, founded by Attar, a former Autodesk R&D executive, and Canadian homebuilder Reza Nasseri, ran its first production line in Edmonton. It then opened a 60,000-square-foot plant in an existing Calgary warehouse, which it has called a flagship hub and a model to replicate in U.S. markets. The Calgary plant was backed in part by a federal contribution from Prairies Economic Development Canada.

Calgary’s anchor customer is the Alberta division of Mattamy Homes, which signed its own multi-year agreement with Promise Robotics to supply single-family, semi-detached and multi-family homes in two master-planned communities. The D.R. Horton deal follows the same template: a multi-year capacity commitment from a large builder, tied to a Promise-run plant.

Phoenix is the test of whether that template travels to the United States. It’s Promise Robotics’ first U.S. production market, a different labor pool, supply chain and building code environment, and a market where the company will need to win business from builders who have their own trade bases and framing crews.

Why a builder would rent capacity instead of building it

For a production builder, the appeal is less about robots than about cycle time and cost per home. Faster, more predictable builds mean inventory turns faster and less capital sits tied up in homes under construction.

Those levers matter more when margins are under pressure. Among the 15 largest homebuilders tracked by ResiClub, 13 giant homebuilders are seeing year-over-year gross margin compression. In that environment, any tool that shaves weeks or labor hours off a build is worth testing.

The Factory-as-a-Service structure also limits the downside. D.R. Horton takes no factory on its balance sheet and carries no fixed overhead if local demand softens. If Promise Robotics’ plants don’t deliver on schedule or on cost, the builder can fall back on its existing trade partners. Promise Robotics carries the capital and operating risk; D.R. Horton carries execution risk on 1,250 homes.

Attar’s comment points to a broader shift he says Promise Robotics is seeing: builders locking in industrial production capacity through multi-year commitments. Two such deals, Mattamy in Alberta and now D.R. Horton, are early evidence for that claim, but not yet a trend.

Ghost in the machine: how AI is haunting the search for the supernatural
item.description:
Ghost hunting has changed in recent years due to AI chatbots, and paranormal enthusiasts are concerned

Ghost hunting is a tech-heavy pursuit. When Amy Waine and Jarrad Cutting investigate haunted locations, they’re loaded up with software of their own design, such as an app that assigns signals from a phone’s sensors to different words in a database. In the age of ChatGPT, the ghost-hunting pair is probing the world of AI. They describe one of their latest inventions, an app called GhostTube Seer, as “the world’s first AI Ghost Hunting tool”.

In the hands of paranormal investigators, scientific tools like EMF meters (used to detect electromagnetic fields) are repurposed to identify changes and anomalies that they believe indicate supernatural activity. Seer is, in many ways, simply an expansion of that practice, another way to scan an empty room and believe that something may be there. The app, which requires a paid monthly subscription, has more than 1m downloads, according to its Google Play store listing.

But for others in the ghost hunting world, AI is an unwelcome presence. Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, AI-generated ghost stories and images of the supernatural have flooded online spaces, so much so that popular forums like the r/Nosleep subreddit, meant for scary stories, have implemented a strict policy against AI-generated material.

item.title: The Guardian view on 50 years of The Selfish Gene: flawed, outdated, yet still a model of truly popular science writing | Editorial
item.description:
Richard Dawkins’ first work has thrilled fans and frustrated critics for five decades. The science has moved on, but any writer looking to supplant its place must learn its lessons

Richard Dawkins’ The Selfish Gene was not predicted to be a success. Its initial print run, published this week in 1976, was just 5,000. It went on to sell millions, and is perhaps the most influential work of pop-science ever. For 50 years, it has been the go-to resource for the layperson seeking to understand evolution.

What accounts for its enduring power? Prof Dawkins’ central claim, that “we are survival machines – robot vehicles blindly programmed to preserve the selfish molecules known as genes” was provocative, stripping the messy stuff of human and other life down to a simple law. And yet the book is primarily concerned with proving that complex, selfless behaviour such as altruism in animals can emerge from these basic “selfish” drives, satisfyingly resolving an apparent paradox. Prof Dawkins – a zoologist by training – also succeeded in conjuring entertaining, vividly drawn vignettes of the lives of animals, from lions and ants to hawks and honeybees, to make his points.

item.title: ‘Don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into’: Delhi women reclaim the outdoors
item.description:
On a wildlife walk in the Indian capital, a group of women share their stories of trying to enjoy nature in a city where strangers feel entitled to harass them

Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”

Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.

item.title: When you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month matters | Hugh Muir
item.description:
There is always debate about the concept’s necessity and efficacy. But with nativists in their pomp, it’s good to focus on who we are and why

  • What forces shaped four generations of Black Britons? | The panel

Pity Black History Month UK, assailed on all sides. Those on the right seek to end the celebration on the basis that it amounts to special treatment for a group that doesn’t deserve it. History should be colour-blind: society should not differentiate, they say. We are not racist, we just want fairness. But often, they are – and they really don’t.

On the other side of the argument are the progressives, notably minority progressives, who say the idea of a month to consider Black history is demeaning because it should already have a year-round place in our teaching and consciousness. There is a further view that any beneficial effect the month once had has been diluted by unimaginative repetition and commercially motivated virtue signalling. Players taking the knee in the Premier League? Been there, done that: yawn!

Hugh Muir is executive editor, Opinion

item.description:
Amid the chaos, havoc and war caused by a capricious and amoral US president, countries are waking up to the dangers of being excluded and abused by America

Never has there been a time when the world has been more interconnected than now. What happens in the secretive inner councils in Tehran, the mountains of south-west Yemen, the steppe of the Donbas, the still bloody wasteland that is Gaza and even the elegant boulevards of Paris and Milan have a common thread.

One cannot understand one set of conflicts without weaving them into another, and it is this very interdependence that is making each problem so contagious, layered and difficult to resolve, leaving the world to live as if trapped inside a pressure cooker on the brink of an explosion.
